title: Ἀπὸ Μυκηνῶν ἐς Σύμην
about: The Catalogue of Ships goes on through the Peloponnese, the western islands, Crete and Rhodes. Agamemnon brings a hundred ships from Mycenae, Corinth and the north coast, and arms himself as the best of the heroes with the most troops; Menelaus brings sixty from Lacedaemon, most eager of all to avenge Helen. Nestor brings ninety from Pylos, where the Muses once maimed Thamyris the Thracian for boasting that he would beat them in song. The Arcadians, who know nothing of the sea, sail in ships Agamemnon gave them under Agapenor; the Epeians of Elis come under four commanders with ten ships each, and Meges brings forty from Dulichium and the Echinae. Odysseus leads the Cephallenians in twelve ships and Thoas the Aetolians in forty, Oeneus and his sons being dead; Idomeneus and Meriones bring eighty from Crete. Tlepolemus, who killed an old kinsman of his father and fled overseas, settles the Rhodians in three parts and is rewarded by Zeus with riches, and the Catalogue turns last to Nireus of Syme, the most beautiful man at Troy after Achilles, who is feeble and has few followers.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ Μυκήνας εἶχον ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον
ἀφνειόν τε Κόρινθον ἐϋκτιμένας τε Κλεωνάς,
sentences.l:
And those who held Mycenae, the well-built citadel,
and rich Corinth, and well-built Cleonae,
sentences.i: And those who held Mycenae, the well-built citadel, and rich Corinth and well-built Cleonae,
sentences.n: A new people in a new paragraph, the men of Mycenae and its neighbourhood. οἳ δέ is ‘and those who’, and the verb is εἶχον ‘held’, the imperfect of ἔχω, with Μυκήνας, Κόρινθον and Κλεωνάς as its objects. Μυκήνας and Κλεωνάς are plural names, ‘Mycenae’ and ‘Cleonae’. ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον ‘the well-built citadel’ is the stock phrase for a walled town, here in apposition to Mycenae; ἐϋκτιμένας is the same adjective in the feminine plural, agreeing with Cleonae. ἀφνειόν is ‘rich’. Place-names are given in their familiar English forms, and the transliteration shows the Greek.

sentences.t:
Ὀρνειάς τ’ ἐνέμοντο Ἀραιθυρέην τ’ ἐρατεινὴν
καὶ Σικυῶν’, ὅθ’ ἄρ’ Ἄδρηστος πρῶτ’ ἐμβασίλευεν,
sentences.l:
and inhabited Orneae and lovely Araethyrea,
and Sicyon, where then Adrastus at first was king,
sentences.i: and inhabited Orneae and lovely Araethyrea, and Sicyon, where Adrastus was king at first,
sentences.n: The sentence goes on with the same people. ἐνέμοντο ‘inhabited’ is the imperfect middle of νέμω and takes Ὀρνειάς (a plural name, ‘Orneae’), Ἀραιθυρέην and Σικυῶν’, the elided accusative Σικυῶνα. ἐρατεινήν is ‘lovely’. ὅθ’ is ὅθι ‘where’, and ἄρ’ a weak ‘then’; ἐμβασίλευεν is the imperfect of ἐμβασιλεύω ‘be king in’. πρῶτ’ is πρῶτα, ‘first’ used as an adverb, and could mean either ‘at first’ or ‘for the first time’; the English takes ‘at first’.

sentences.t:
οἵ θ’ Ὑπερησίην τε καὶ αἰπεινὴν Γονόεσσαν
Πελλήνην τ’ εἶχον ἠδ’ Αἴγιον ἀμφενέμοντο
Αἰγιαλόν τ’ ἀνὰ πάντα καὶ ἀμφ’ Ἑλίκην εὐρεῖαν,
sentences.l:
and who held Hyperesia and steep Gonoessa
and Pellene, and inhabited around Aegium,
and all through Aegialus and about broad Helice,
sentences.i: and those who held Hyperesia and steep Gonoessa and Pellene, and inhabited the country around Aegium, and all through Aegialus and about broad Helice,
sentences.n: Two more verbs: εἶχον ‘held’ takes Ὑπερησίην, Γονόεσσαν and Πελλήνην, and ἀμφενέμοντο, the imperfect middle of ἀμφινέμομαι ‘inhabit around’, takes Αἴγιον. αἰπεινήν is ‘steep’, the feminine of αἰπεινός (the Odyssey’s αἰπύς ‘steep’ is the same root), and εὐρεῖαν ‘broad’. Αἰγιαλόν τ’ ἀνὰ πάντα, with ἀνά after its noun, is ‘and all through Aegialus’, Αἰγιαλός being the name of the north coast of the Peloponnese and also the ordinary word for ‘seashore’; ἀμφ’ Ἑλίκην εὐρεῖαν is ‘about broad Helice’, with ἀμφί and the accusative.

sentences.t:
τῶν ἑκατὸν νηῶν ἦρχε κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
Ἀτρεΐδης·
sentences.l:
Of these, of a hundred ships, was leading lord Agamemnon,
Atreus’-son;
sentences.i: Of these lord Agamemnon, the son of Atreus, led a hundred ships;
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s own force, the largest of the Catalogue. τῶν ἑκατὸν νηῶν is ‘of these hundred ships’, with τῶν agreeing with νηῶν (the epic genitive plural of ναῦς), and the whole is the genitive after ἦρχε ‘led’, since ἄρχω takes the genitive. κρείων is ‘lord’, and Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’ is his patronymic, standing here as a second title after the name. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 577.

sentences.t:
ἅμα τῷ γε πολὺ πλεῖστοι καὶ ἄριστοι
λαοὶ ἕποντ’·
sentences.l:
with him, by far the most numerous and the best,
people followed;
sentences.i: With him followed troops by far the most numerous and the best;
sentences.n: ἅμα ‘along with’ takes the dative τῷ ‘him’, with γε to stress it. πολὺ πλεῖστοι ‘by far the most numerous’: πολύ strengthens the superlative πλεῖστοι (from πολύς), and ἄριστοι ‘best’ is the superlative of ἀγαθός; both agree with λαοί, the plural of λαός ‘people’, here the fighting men of an army, which the English calls ‘troops’. ἕποντ’ is ἕποντο, the unaugmented imperfect middle of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. The unit begins in the middle of line 577 and ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 578.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ αὐτὸς ἐδύσετο νώροπα χαλκὸν
κυδιόων, πᾶσιν δὲ μετέπρεπεν ἡρώεσσιν
οὕνεκ’ ἄριστος ἔην πολὺ δὲ πλείστους ἄγε λαούς.
sentences.l:
and he himself put on the flashing bronze,
glorying, and was conspicuous among all the heroes
because the best he was, and by far the most people he brought.
sentences.i: and he himself put on the flashing bronze, glorying, and was conspicuous among all the heroes, because he was the best and brought by far the most troops.
sentences.n: Agamemnon arms in person. ἐν … ἐδύσετο is one verb with its preverb ἐν set apart from it (tmesis), ‘put on’, an epic aorist middle of δύω; the object is νώροπα χαλκόν, ‘the flashing bronze’, i.e. his armour. νώροπα is a stock epithet whose meaning is not known, ‘flashing’ being the traditional guess, and the Odyssey has the same phrase. κυδιόων is the participle of κυδιάω, from κῦδος ‘glory’, and has no object. μετέπρεπεν is the imperfect of μεταπρέπω ‘be conspicuous among’, with the epic dative πᾶσιν ἡρώεσσιν ‘all the heroes’. οὕνεκ’ is ‘because’, ἔην the epic imperfect of εἰμί, and ἄγε the unaugmented imperfect of ἄγω ‘bring’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ εἶχον κοίλην Λακεδαίμονα κητώεσσαν,
Φᾶρίν τε Σπάρτην τε πολυτρήρωνά τε Μέσσην,
sentences.l:
And those who held hollow Lacedaemon, full-of-ravines,
and Pharis and Sparta and Messe, rich in doves,
sentences.i: And those who held hollow Lacedaemon, land of many ravines, and Pharis, Sparta, and Messe, rich in doves,
sentences.n: Menelaus’ people, in a new paragraph. οἳ δ’ εἶχον is ‘and those who held’. κοίλην Λακεδαίμονα κητώεσσαν ‘hollow Lacedaemon, full of ravines’ is the same phrase the Odyssey opens its fourth book with, and keeps the English given there; κητώεσσαν is an adjective whose meaning is not certain (‘full of ravines’ is the traditional sense), and the Odyssey’s ‘land of many ravines’ is not decided here either. Φᾶρίν, Σπάρτην and Μέσσην are the other places, accusatives. πολυτρήρωνα is ‘rich in doves’, taking τρήρων as the noun ‘dove’ as in Thisbe at 502.

sentences.t:
Βρυσειάς τ’ ἐνέμοντο καὶ Αὐγειὰς ἐρατεινάς,
οἵ τ’ ἄρ’ Ἀμύκλας εἶχον Ἕλος τ’ ἔφαλον πτολίεθρον,
οἵ τε Λάαν εἶχον ἠδ’ Οἴτυλον ἀμφενέμοντο,
sentences.l:
and inhabited Bryseiae and lovely Augeiae,
and who held Amyclae and Helos, a citadel by the sea,
and who held Laas and inhabited around Oetylus,
sentences.i: and inhabited Bryseiae and lovely Augeiae, and those who held Amyclae and Helos, a citadel by the sea, and those who held Laas and inhabited the country around Oetylus,
sentences.n: Three more clauses on the same pattern. Βρυσειάς and Αὐγειάς are plural names, ‘Bryseiae’ and ‘Augeiae’ (the same word as the Locrian Augeiae at 532), and ἐρατεινάς is ‘lovely’. οἵ τ’ ἄρ’ … εἶχον is ‘and those who held’, with a weak ἄρ’ left untranslated, taking Ἀμύκλας ‘Amyclae’ and Ἕλος; ἔφαλον πτολίεθρον is ‘a citadel by the sea’, ἔφαλον ‘by the sea’ (as with Cerinthus at 538) and πτολίεθρον ‘citadel’. Λάαν is ‘Laas’, and Οἴτυλον ἀμφενέμοντο is ‘inhabited around Oetylus’, the verb as at 574.

sentences.t:
τῶν οἱ ἀδελφεὸς ἦρχε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος
ἑξήκοντα νεῶν·
sentences.l:
Of these his brother was leading, good at the war-cry, Menelaus,
sixty ships;
sentences.i: Of these his brother Menelaus, good at the war-cry, led sixty ships;
sentences.n: Menelaus. τῶν is ‘of these’; οἱ is the enclitic dative ‘to him’, and with ἀδελφεός (the epic form of ἀδελφός ‘brother’) it means ‘his brother’, Agamemnon’s. ἦρχε takes the genitive ἑξήκοντα νεῶν ‘of sixty ships’, as at 576. βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is Menelaus’ stock epithet, βοήν an accusative of respect, and the Odyssey gives it to him in the same words. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 587.

sentences.t: ἀπάτερθε δὲ θωρήσσοντο·
sentences.l: and apart they were arming themselves;
sentences.i: and they armed themselves apart;
sentences.n: ἀπάτερθε is ‘apart’, here apart from Agamemnon’s force, and θωρήσσοντο is the imperfect middle of θωρήσσω ‘arm’, plural because the subject is Menelaus’ whole people, not he alone. The unit is short because it lies between two ano teleiai in the same line.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ αὐτὸς κίεν ᾗσι προθυμίῃσι πεποιθὼς
ὀτρύνων πόλεμον δέ·
sentences.l:
and among them he himself went, in his own eagerness trusting,
urging them to war;
sentences.i: and he himself went among them, trusting in his own eagerness, urging them to war;
sentences.n: Menelaus in person, as Agamemnon was at 578. ἐν δ’ αὐτός is ‘and among them he himself’, ἐν standing alone as an adverb, and κίεν is the imperfect of κίω ‘go’. ᾗσι is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative, agreeing with the dative plural προθυμίῃσι (προθυμία ‘eagerness’), which is what he trusts, after the perfect participle πεποιθώς (πείθομαι ‘trust’). ὀτρύνων ‘urging’ has no object in the Greek, and the English supplies ‘them’. πόλεμον δέ is πόλεμον with the suffix -δε ‘towards’, ‘to war’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 589.

sentences.t:
μάλιστα δὲ ἵετο θυμῷ
τίσασθαι Ἑλένης ὁρμήματά τε στοναχάς τε.
sentences.l:
and most of all he was eager in heart
to avenge Helen’s strivings and groans.
sentences.i: and most of all he was eager in heart to avenge Helen’s strivings and groans.
sentences.n: The reason for Menelaus’ zeal. μάλιστα ‘most of all’ is the superlative of μάλα; ἵετο is the imperfect of ἵεμαι ‘be eager’ (the middle of ἵημι ‘send’), with the dative θυμῷ ‘in heart’ and the infinitive τίσασθαι, the aorist middle of τίνω in the sense ‘exact a penalty for, avenge’, a different verb from τίω ‘honour’. Its objects are Ἑλένης ὁρμήματα ‘Helen’s strivings’ and στοναχάς ‘groans’ (στοναχή), paired by τε … τε. The Greek does not say whose strivings: her own struggles or the efforts made for her are both possible, and the English leaves it open, as at 356. The unit begins in the middle of line 589.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ Πύλον τ’ ἐνέμοντο καὶ Ἀρήνην ἐρατεινὴν
καὶ Θρύον Ἀλφειοῖο πόρον καὶ ἐΰκτιτον Αἰπὺ
καὶ Κυπαρισσήεντα καὶ Ἀμφιγένειαν ἔναιον
καὶ Πτελεὸν καὶ Ἕλος καὶ Δώριον,
sentences.l:
And those who Pylos inhabited and lovely Arene
and Thryum, the ford of the Alpheus, and well-founded Aepy
and Cyparisseis and Amphigeneia dwelt in
and Pteleum and Helos and Dorium,
sentences.i: And those who inhabited Pylos and lovely Arene, Thryum, the ford of the Alpheus, and well-founded Aepy, and dwelt in Cyparisseis and Amphigeneia, Pteleum, Helos and Dorium,
sentences.n: The Pylians, in a new paragraph. ἐνέμοντο ‘inhabited’ governs Πύλον and Ἀρήνην ἐρατεινήν ‘lovely Arene’; ἔναιον, the imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell in’, ends 593 and governs the two names before it and those of 594 after it; Θρύον and Αἰπύ could go with either verb, and the English gives them to the first. Θρύον Ἀλφειοῖο πόρον is ‘Thryum, the ford of the Alpheus’, with the epic genitive Ἀλφειοῖο. ἐΰκτιτον ‘well-founded’ is from κτίζω ‘found’, a different word from the ἐϋκτίμενον ‘well-built’ of 569. Αἰπύ is the neuter of αἰπύς ‘steep’ used as a name, ‘Aepy’. Κυπαρισσήεντα is an adjective, ‘abounding in cypresses’, used as a name, ‘Cyparisseis’. This Helos is not the Laconian one of 584. The unit ends at the comma in the middle of 594.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά τε Μοῦσαι
ἀντόμεναι Θάμυριν τὸν Θρήϊκα παῦσαν ἀοιδῆς
Οἰχαλίηθεν ἰόντα παρ’ Εὐρύτου Οἰχαλιῆος·
sentences.i: where the Muses met Thamyris the Thracian and stopped him from singing, as he was on his way from Oechalia, from Eurytus the Oechalian;
sentences.n: A story told about the place. ἔνθά τε is ‘where’, with the epic τε that links a familiar story. The Muses are the subject of παῦσαν, the unaugmented aorist of παύω ‘stop’, which takes the genitive ἀοιδῆς ‘from song’; its object is Θάμυριν τὸν Θρήϊκα ‘Thamyris the Thracian’, and ἀντόμεναι is the participle of ἀντάω ‘meet’. Οἰχαλίηθεν is ‘from Oechalia’ (the suffix -θεν ‘from’), ἰόντα ‘going’ the participle of εἶμι, and παρ’ Εὐρύτου Οἰχαλιῆος is ‘from Eurytus the Oechalian’, παρά with the genitive meaning ‘from beside’. This Eurytus is a different man from the Eurytus of 621.

sentences.t:
στεῦτο γὰρ εὐχόμενος νικησέμεν εἴ περ ἂν αὐταὶ
Μοῦσαι ἀείδοιεν κοῦραι Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο·
sentences.l:
for he declared, boasting, that he would win, even if themselves
the Muses should sing, the daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus;
sentences.i: for he claimed, in his boasting, that he would win, even if the Muses themselves, the daughters of aegis-bearing Zeus, should sing;
sentences.n: Why they stopped him. στεῦτο is the imperfect of στεῦται, a rare verb of solemn assertion, ‘he declared’; the Odyssey has it as ‘he declares, claims’ (the στεῦτο at Odyssey 11.584, ‘he stood’, is another sense). εὐχόμενος here is ‘boasting’, as with a claim, not ‘praying’, and νικησέμεν is the future infinitive of νικάω ‘win’. εἴ περ ἂν … ἀείδοιεν is ‘even if … should sing’, an optative; αὐταί ‘themselves’ is feminine plural, with Μοῦσαι, and κοῦραι ‘girls’ is in apposition, ‘daughters’ of Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο, ‘aegis-bearing Zeus’ (epic genitive -οιο).

sentences.t:
αἳ δὲ χολωσάμεναι πηρὸν θέσαν, αὐτὰρ ἀοιδὴν
θεσπεσίην ἀφέλοντο καὶ ἐκλέλαθον κιθαριστύν·
sentences.l:
and they, having been angered, made him maimed, and the song
wondrous took away from him and made him forget lyre-playing;
sentences.i: and in their anger they maimed him, took away his wondrous song, and made him forget his lyre-playing;
sentences.n: What the Muses did. αἳ δέ is ‘and they’, the Muses; χολωσάμεναι is the aorist participle of χολόομαι ‘be angered’, from χόλος ‘anger’. θέσαν is the unaugmented aorist of τίθημι, and with πηρόν it means ‘made (him) maimed’; the object is understood, and πηρός can mean crippled or blind, which the Greek does not decide. ἀοιδὴν θεσπεσίην ‘wondrous song’ is the object of ἀφέλοντο, the aorist middle of ἀφαιρέω ‘take away’, so ‘took away from him’. ἐκλέλαθον is a reduplicated aorist of ἐκλανθάνω in its causative sense ‘made (him) forget’, and κιθαριστύν is ‘lyre-playing’, a rare noun.

sentences.t: τῶν αὖθ’ ἡγεμόνευε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.l: Of these again was leader the Gerenian horseman Nestor;
sentences.i: Of these, in turn, the Gerenian horseman Nestor was the leader;
sentences.n: The leader formula of 540, 552 and 563: τῶν αὖθ’ ἡγεμόνευε ‘of these again was leader’, αὖθ’ being a form of αὖθις ‘again, in turn’. Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ ‘the Gerenian horseman Nestor’ is his standing name-epithet, the same in the Odyssey; why he is called Γερήνιος is disputed (a place Gerenia, or a word meaning ‘old’), and the English does not decide. ἱππότα is the epic nominative of ἱππότης ‘horseman’.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἐνενήκοντα γλαφυραὶ νέες ἐστιχόωντο.
sentences.l: and for him ninety hollow ships went in line.
sentences.i: and ninety hollow ships went in line with him.
sentences.n: The entry closes with its number, as at 516, which has the same ending. τῷ is ‘to him, with him’, ἐνενήκοντα ‘ninety’, and γλαφυραί ‘hollow’ the stock epithet of ships. νέες is the epic nominative plural of ναῦς, and ἐστιχόωντο the imperfect of στιχάομαι ‘go in line’, with the stretched ending -όω-; the other entries here mostly close with ἕποντο.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἔχον Ἀρκαδίην ὑπὸ Κυλλήνης ὄρος αἰπὺ
Αἰπύτιον παρὰ τύμβον ἵν’ ἀνέρες ἀγχιμαχηταί,
sentences.l:
And those who held Arcadia beneath the steep mountain of Cyllene,
by the Aepytian tomb, where the men are close-fighters,
sentences.i: And those who held Arcadia beneath the steep mountain of Cyllene, by the Aepytian tomb, where the men are fighters at close quarters,
sentences.n: The Arcadians, in a new paragraph. οἳ δ’ ἔχον is ‘and those who held’, with Ἀρκαδίην the Ionic form of the name. ὑπὸ … ὄρος αἰπύ is ‘beneath the steep mountain’, ὑπό with the accusative, and Κυλλήνης is the genitive of the mountain’s name, ‘of Cyllene’. Αἰπύτιον παρὰ τύμβον is ‘by the Aepytian tomb’, the tomb of Aepytus, with the adjective Αἰπύτιος and παρά with the accusative. ἵν’ is ἵνα ‘where’. ἀνέρες is the epic ἄνδρες ‘men’; ἀγχιμαχηταί ‘close-fighters’ is built from ἀγχί ‘near’ and μάχομαι ‘fight’, and the Greek has no verb ‘are’.

sentences.t:
οἳ Φενεόν τ’ ἐνέμοντο καὶ Ὀρχομενὸν πολύμηλον
Ῥίπην τε Στρατίην τε καὶ ἠνεμόεσσαν Ἐνίσπην
καὶ Τεγέην εἶχον καὶ Μαντινέην ἐρατεινὴν
Στύμφηλόν τ’ εἶχον καὶ Παρρασίην ἐνέμοντο,
sentences.l:
who inhabited Pheneus and Orchomenus, rich in flocks,
and Rhipe and Stratie and windy Enispe,
and held Tegea and lovely Mantinea,
and held Stymphelus and inhabited Parrhasia,
sentences.i: who inhabited Pheneus and Orchomenus, rich in flocks, and Rhipe, Stratie and windy Enispe, and held Tegea and lovely Mantinea, and held Stymphelus and inhabited Parrhasia,
sentences.n: The towns of Arcadia. The relative οἳ continues the people of 603, and the verbs alternate with the places: ἐνέμοντο ‘inhabited’ (605, 608) and εἶχον ‘held’ (607, 608). Ὀρχομενόν here is the Arcadian Orchomenus, not the Minyan one of 511. πολύμηλον is ‘rich in flocks’, from πολύ- ‘many’ and μῆλον ‘sheep, goat’, as the Odyssey uses μῆλα; ἠνεμόεσσαν ‘windy’ is the feminine accusative of ἠνεμόεις, from ἄνεμος ‘wind’; ἐρατεινήν is ‘lovely’. Ῥίπην, Στρατίην and Ἐνίσπην are Ionic forms, accusatives, and Στύμφηλον and Παρρασίην the last two names.

sentences.t:
τῶν ἦρχ’ Ἀγκαίοιο πάϊς κρείων Ἀγαπήνωρ
ἑξήκοντα νεῶν·
sentences.l:
Of these was leading the son of Ancaeus, lord Agapenor,
of sixty ships;
sentences.i: Of these lord Agapenor, the son of Ancaeus, led sixty ships;
sentences.n: Their commander. τῶν ἦρχ’ is ‘of these was leading’, ἦρχ’ standing for ἦρχε with its vowel dropped before the next word. Ἀγκαίοιο is the epic genitive -οιο of Ἀγκαῖος, πάϊς the epic form of παῖς ‘son’, and κρείων ‘lord’; ἑξήκοντα νεῶν ‘of sixty ships’ is the genitive after ἦρχε, as at 576 and 586. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 610.

sentences.t:
πολέες δ’ ἐν νηῒ ἑκάστῃ
Ἀρκάδες ἄνδρες ἔβαινον ἐπιστάμενοι πολεμίζειν.
sentences.l:
and many in each ship
Arcadian men were embarking, knowing how to wage war.
sentences.i: and in each ship many Arcadian men were embarking, knowing how to wage war.
sentences.n: The crews. πολέες is the epic nominative plural of πολύς ‘many’; ἐν νηῒ ἑκάστῃ is ‘in each ship’, with the epic dative νηΐ (the diaeresis marks the vowels as separate syllables). ἔβαινον is the imperfect of βαίνω ‘go, embark’, as at 510, where the form is βαῖνον without the augment. Ἀρκάδες ἄνδρες is ‘Arcadian men’. ἐπιστάμενοι is the participle of ἐπίσταμαι ‘know how to’, with the infinitive πολεμίζειν ‘wage war’. The unit begins in the middle of line 610.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς γάρ σφιν δῶκεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους περάαν ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον
Ἀτρεΐδης, ἐπεὶ οὔ σφι θαλάσσια ἔργα μεμήλει.
sentences.l:
For himself had given them the lord of men, Agamemnon,
well-benched ships to cross over the wine-faced open-sea,
Atreus’-son, since for them the works of the sea were no care.
sentences.i: For Agamemnon himself, lord of men, the son of Atreus, had given them well-benched ships to cross the sea that has the look of wine, since the work of the sea was no concern of theirs.
sentences.n: Why men from an inland country have ships. γάρ explains 610–611, and αὐτός ‘himself’ stresses that Agamemnon supplied them. δῶκεν is the aorist of δίδωμι, with σφιν ‘to them’ and the infinitive περάαν, the epic form of περᾶν ‘to cross’. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is the stock epithet; Ἀτρεΐδης, ‘son of Atreus’, opens line 614 as a second title. νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους is ‘well-benched ships’, and οἴνοπα πόντον ‘the wine-faced sea’, the Odyssey’s sea that looks like wine; Greek colour words are not ours. θαλάσσια ἔργα is ‘works of the sea’, and μεμήλει is the pluperfect of μέλω ‘be a care to’ used as an imperfect, with the dative σφι.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἄρα Βουπράσιόν τε καὶ Ἤλιδα δῖαν ἔναιον
ὅσσον ἐφ’ Ὑρμίνη καὶ Μύρσινος ἐσχατόωσα
πέτρη τ’ Ὠλενίη καὶ Ἀλήσιον ἐντὸς ἐέργει,
sentences.l:
And those who then dwelt in Buprasium and heavenly Elis,
as much as Hyrmine and Myrsinus, lying at the edge,
and the Olenian rock and Aleisium shut in within,
sentences.i: And those who dwelt in Buprasium and heavenly Elis, all the land that Hyrmine and Myrsinus, lying at the edge, and the Olenian rock and Aleisium shut in,
sentences.n: The Epeians of Elis, in a new paragraph, and the border of their land. οἳ δ’ ἄρα … ἔναιον is ‘and those who dwelt in’, taking Βουπράσιον and Ἤλιδα δῖαν ‘heavenly Elis’, δῖαν the stock epithet, as the Odyssey has it of Lacedaemon. Then ὅσσον … ἐέργει ‘as much as … shut in’. The construction is compressed, and how ἐφ’ (ἐπί) attaches is not clear; the English takes the four places as the boundary that shuts in the Epeians’ land. Μύρσινος takes the feminine ἐσχατόωσα ‘lying at the edge’, and ἐέργει, the epic form of εἴργει ‘shuts in’, is singular although its subjects are several.

sentences.t:
τῶν αὖ τέσσαρες ἀρχοὶ ἔσαν, δέκα δ’ ἀνδρὶ ἑκάστῳ
νῆες ἕποντο θοαί, πολέες δ’ ἔμβαινον Ἐπειοί.
sentences.l:
Of these again four were commanders, and ten to each man
ships followed, swift, and many Epeians were embarking.
sentences.i: Of these, in turn, there were four commanders, and ten swift ships followed each man, and many Epeians were embarking.
sentences.n: Their four commanders and the ships. τῶν αὖ is ‘of these again’; ἀρχοί ‘commanders’ is the plural of ἀρχός, and ἔσαν is ἦσαν ‘were’. ἀνδρὶ ἑκάστῳ ‘to each man’ is the dative with νῆες ἕποντο ‘ships followed’, so each of the four has ten, forty in all, which the Greek does not add. θοαί ‘swift’ is the stock epithet of ships, ἔμβαινον the imperfect of ἐμβαίνω ‘embark’, and Ἐπειοί ‘Epeians’ the people of Elis.

sentences.t:
τῶν μὲν ἄρ’ Ἀμφίμαχος καὶ Θάλπιος ἡγησάσθην
υἷες ὃ μὲν Κτεάτου, ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ Εὐρύτου, Ἀκτορίωνε·
sentences.l:
Of these, then, Amphimachus and Thalpius led,
sons, the one of Cteatus, and the other of Eurytus, the two of Actor’s line;
sentences.i: Of these, then, Amphimachus and Thalpius led, sons, the one of Cteatus and the other of Eurytus, the pair of Actor’s line;
sentences.n: Two of the four. τῶν μὲν ἄρ’ is ‘of these, then’, and ἡγησάσθην is the dual aorist of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’, the Greek dual again, for a pair. υἷες is ‘sons’, and ὃ μὲν … ὃ δ’ ‘the one … the other’ is the article used as a pronoun, so Amphimachus is the son of Cteatus and Thalpius of Eurytus. Ἀκτορίωνε is a dual patronymic from Actor, ‘the two of Actor’s line’; the two leaders are sons of Cteatus and Eurytus, not of Actor himself, and the Greek does not say how the line runs. This Eurytus is not the king of Oechalia of 596.

sentences.t: τῶν δ’ Ἀμαρυγκεΐδης ἦρχε κρατερὸς Διώρης·
sentences.l: And of these Amarynceus’-son was leading, strong Diores;
sentences.i: And of these strong Diores, the son of Amarynceus, led;
sentences.n: The third commander. τῶν δ’ is ‘and of these’. Ἀμαρυγκεΐδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Amarynceus’, put before the name Διώρης, and κρατερός ‘strong’ is the stock epithet. ἦρχε ‘led’ takes the genitive τῶν.

sentences.t:
τῶν δὲ τετάρτων ἦρχε Πολύξεινος θεοειδὴς
υἱὸς Ἀγασθένεος Αὐγηϊάδαο ἄνακτος.
sentences.l:
And of the fourth was leading Polyxeinus, godlike-in-form,
son of Agasthenes, Augeas’-son, the lord.
sentences.i: And the fourth was led by Polyxeinus, godlike in form, the son of lord Agasthenes, Augeas’ son.
sentences.n: The fourth commander. τετάρτων is the genitive plural of τέταρτος ‘fourth’, with the noun (the fourth commander’s company) left out, and ἦρχε takes it as its genitive. θεοειδής is ‘godlike in form’, the Odyssey’s epithet. Ἀγασθένεος is the genitive of Ἀγασθένης, with ἄνακτος ‘lord’ agreeing with it, and Αὐγηϊάδαο is a patronymic with the epic genitive -αο, ‘son of Augeas’, naming Agasthenes’ father, so that Polyxeinus is Augeas’ grandson.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐκ Δουλιχίοιο Ἐχινάων θ’ ἱεράων
νήσων, αἳ ναίουσι πέρην ἁλὸς Ἤλιδος ἄντα,
sentences.l:
And those from Dulichium and the sacred Echinae
islands, which lie across the sea, opposite Elis,
sentences.i: And those from Dulichium and the sacred Echinae, islands that lie across the sea, facing Elis,
sentences.n: The island people, in a new paragraph. οἳ δ’ ἐκ Δουλιχίοιο is ‘and those from Dulichium’, with the epic genitive -οιο and no verb. Ἐχινάων … ἱεράων νήσων is ‘of the sacred Echinae islands’, with the epic genitive plural -άων; ἱερός is ‘sacred’, and νήσων comes after the name. αἳ ναίουσι is ‘which dwell’, said of islands and meaning ‘which lie’. πέρην governs ἁλός, ‘across the sea’, and ἄντα governs Ἤλιδος, ‘facing Elis’. Dulichium is the island the Odyssey also names with Same and Zacynthus.

sentences.t:
τῶν αὖθ’ ἡγεμόνευε Μέγης ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ
Φυλεΐδης, ὃν τίκτε Διῒ φίλος ἱππότα Φυλεύς,
sentences.l:
Of these again was leader Meges, the equal of Ares,
Phyleus’-son, whom begot dear to Zeus the horseman Phyleus,
sentences.i: Of these, in turn, Meges, the equal of Ares, the son of Phyleus, was the leader, whom Phyleus the horseman, dear to Zeus, begot,
sentences.n: The leader formula of 601: τῶν αὖθ’ ἡγεμόνευε ‘of these again was leader’. ἀτάλαντος Ἄρηϊ is ‘the equal of Ares’, ἀτάλαντος ‘equal in weight’ taking the dative, as Odysseus is ‘equal of Zeus in cunning’ at 169 and again at 636. Φυλεΐδης ‘son of Phyleus’ is a patronymic, and ὃν τίκτε … Φυλεύς is ‘whom Phyleus begot’: τίκτε is the unaugmented imperfect of τίκτω, ‘bear’ of a mother and ‘beget’ of a father. Διῒ φίλος ‘dear to Zeus’ has the dative with its diaeresis, and ἱππότα ‘horseman’ is the epithet Nestor has at 601.

sentences.t: ὅς ποτε Δουλίχιον δ’ ἀπενάσσατο πατρὶ χολωθείς·
sentences.l: who once to Dulichium removed himself, having been angered with his father;
sentences.i: who once removed himself to Dulichium, in anger at his father;
sentences.n: Why Phyleus lives at Dulichium. ὅς is ‘who’, ποτε ‘once’, and Δουλίχιον δ’ is Δουλίχιον with the suffix -δε ‘to’. ἀπενάσσατο is the aorist middle of ἀπονάσσω, ‘settle away, remove oneself’, related to ναίω ‘dwell’. χολωθείς is the aorist passive participle of χολόω ‘anger’, with the dative πατρί ‘with his father’.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἅμα τεσσαράκοντα μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο.
sentences.l: And with him forty black ships followed.
sentences.i: And with him forty black ships followed.
sentences.n: The closing formula of an entry, as at 545 and in the first half of 534: τῷ δ’ ἅμα ‘and with him’ (Meges), τεσσαράκοντα ‘forty’, μέλαιναι νῆες ‘black ships’, ἕποντο ‘followed’. The same line comes again at 644.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς ἦγε Κεφαλλῆνας μεγαθύμους,
sentences.l: But Odysseus brought the great-hearted Cephallenians,
sentences.i: But Odysseus brought the great-hearted Cephallenians,
sentences.n: Odysseus and the Cephallenians, in a new paragraph. αὐτάρ ‘but’ opens the entry, and ἦγε is the imperfect of ἄγω ‘bring’, kept apart in English from ἄρχω ‘lead’. Κεφαλλῆνας is the accusative plural of Κεφαλλήν, and μεγαθύμους ‘great-hearted’ the stock epithet. The places they hold follow in the relative clauses of 632–635.

sentences.t:
οἵ ῥ’ Ἰθάκην εἶχον καὶ Νήριτον εἰνοσίφυλλον
καὶ Κροκύλει’ ἐνέμοντο καὶ Αἰγίλιπα τρηχεῖαν,
sentences.l:
who held Ithaca and Neriton, leaf-shaking,
and inhabited Crocylea and rough Aegilips,
sentences.i: who held Ithaca and leaf-shaking Neriton, and inhabited Crocylea and rough Aegilips,
sentences.n: The kingdom of Odysseus. οἵ ῥ’ is ‘who’ (ῥα is a weak particle, left untranslated). εἶχον ‘held’ takes Ἰθάκην and Νήριτον εἰνοσίφυλλον ‘leaf-shaking Neriton’, the mountain of Ithaca of Odyssey 9.21–22, εἰνοσίφυλλον being ἔνοσις ‘shaking’ and φύλλον ‘leaf’. ἐνέμοντο ‘inhabited’ takes Κροκύλει’, the elided neuter plural Κροκύλεια, and Αἰγίλιπα, the accusative of Αἴγιλιψ, with τρηχεῖαν ‘rough’ (τρηχύς, the Odyssey’s word for the ground of Ithaca). Where Crocylea and Aegilips lay is not certainly known.

sentences.t:
οἵ τε Ζάκυνθον ἔχον ἠδ’ οἳ Σάμον ἀμφενέμοντο,
οἵ τ’ ἤπειρον ἔχον ἠδ’ ἀντιπέραι’ ἐνέμοντο·
sentences.l:
and who held Zacynthus, and who inhabited around Samos,
and who held the mainland and inhabited the lands over against it;
sentences.i: and those who held Zacynthus and those who inhabited the country around Samos, and those who held the mainland and inhabited the lands opposite it;
sentences.n: The rest of Odysseus’ realm. οἵ τε … ἔχον is ‘and those who held’, and ἠδ’ οἳ … ἀμφενέμοντο ‘and those who inhabited around’. Ζάκυνθον is Zacynthus, an island, and Σάμον is Samos, probably the island the Odyssey calls Same, not the Samos of Ionia. ἤπειρον is ‘the mainland’, and ἀντιπέραι’, the elided neuter plural ἀντιπέραια, is ‘the lands opposite’, the places on the far shore, with ἐνέμοντο ‘inhabited’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: τῶν μὲν Ὀδυσσεὺς ἦρχε Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντος·
sentences.l: Of these Odysseus was leading, the equal of Zeus in cunning;
sentences.i: Of these Odysseus led, the equal of Zeus in cunning;
sentences.n: τῶν μὲν Ὀδυσσεὺς ἦρχε is ‘of these Odysseus was leading’. Διὶ μῆτιν ἀτάλαντος is ‘the equal of Zeus in cunning’: ἀτάλαντος ‘equal in weight’ takes the dative Διΐ, and μῆτιν is an accusative of respect, ‘in cunning’, as in the phrase used of him at 169. μῆτις is the quality of mind that sets Odysseus apart, and the epithet is translated the same each time.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἅμα νῆες ἕποντο δυώδεκα μιλτοπάρῃοι.
sentences.l: And with him ships followed, twelve, red-cheeked.
sentences.i: And with him twelve red-cheeked ships followed.
sentences.n: The closing formula of an entry with its words in a different order: τῷ δ’ ἅμα ‘and with him’, νῆες ἕποντο ‘ships followed’, then the number and the epithet, δυώδεκα ‘twelve’ and μιλτοπάρῃοι ‘red-cheeked’. μιλτοπάρῃος is built on μίλτος ‘red ochre’ and παρῃά ‘cheek’; a ship’s cheeks are the sides of her bow, which the usual explanation says were painted red. The Odyssey has the word of ships in the same way.

sentences.t:
Αἰτωλῶν δ’ ἡγεῖτο Θόας Ἀνδραίμονος υἱός,
οἳ Πλευρῶν’ ἐνέμοντο καὶ Ὤλενον ἠδὲ Πυλήνην
Χαλκίδα τ’ ἀγχίαλον Καλυδῶνά τε πετρήεσσαν·
sentences.i: And Thoas, the son of Andraemon, led the Aetolians, who inhabited Pleuron, Olenus and Pylene, Chalcis near the sea and rocky Calydon;
sentences.n: The Aetolians, in a new paragraph. Αἰτωλῶν δ’ ἡγεῖτο is ‘and of the Aetolians was leading’ (ἡγεῖτο the imperfect of ἡγέομαι, with the genitive), Θόας Ἀνδραίμονος υἱός ‘Thoas, son of Andraemon’. οἳ … ἐνέμοντο ‘who inhabited’ takes Πλευρῶν’ (the elided accusative Πλευρῶνα), Ὤλενον, Πυλήνην, Χαλκίδα and Καλυδῶνα. ἀγχίαλον is ‘near the sea’, from ἀγχί ‘near’ and ἅλς ‘sea’, kept apart from ἔφαλον ‘by the sea’; this Chalcis is an Aetolian town, not the Chalcis of Euboea at 537. πετρήεσσαν ‘rocky’ is the feminine accusative of πετρήεις, as at 496.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ Οἰνῆος μεγαλήτορος υἱέες ἦσαν,
οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτ’ αὐτὸς ἔην, θάνε δὲ ξανθὸς Μελέαγρος·
sentences.l:
For no longer were the sons of great-spirited Oeneus alive,
nor was he himself any more, and fair-haired Meleager had died;
sentences.i: for the sons of great-spirited Oeneus were no longer alive, nor was he himself, and fair-haired Meleager had died;
sentences.n: Why Thoas is the leader. ἦσαν ‘were’ means ‘were alive, existed’, and so does ἔην (the epic ἦν) in the next line, with Oeneus as its subject: οὐδ’ ἄρ’ ἔτ’ αὐτὸς ἔην is ‘nor was he himself any more’. υἱέες is the epic nominative plural of υἱός. Οἰνῆος μεγαλήτορος is the epic genitive of Οἰνεύς with μεγαλήτορος ‘great-spirited’. θάνε is the unaugmented aorist of θνῄσκω ‘die’, and ξανθός ‘fair-haired’ is the epithet the Odyssey gives Menelaus. Meleager is one of Oeneus’ sons.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἐπὶ πάντ’ ἐτέταλτο ἀνασσέμεν Αἰτωλοῖσι·
sentences.l: and to him everything had been enjoined, to be lord over the Aetolians;
sentences.i: and everything had been laid upon him: to rule the Aetolians;
sentences.n: τῷ δ’ ἐπὶ … ἐτέταλτο is one verb with ἐπί set apart from it (tmesis), the pluperfect passive of ἐπιτέλλω ‘enjoin, lay a charge on’, the verb of ἔτελλε at 1.25; τῷ is ‘to him’, and πάντ’ ‘everything’. What was enjoined is the infinitive ἀνασσέμεν, the epic form of ἀνάσσειν ‘be lord’, with the dative Αἰτωλοῖσι ‘over the Aetolians’. The Greek says only that the rule had been laid on Thoas, not by whom.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἅμα τεσσαράκοντα μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο.
sentences.l: And with him forty black ships followed.
sentences.i: And with him forty black ships followed.
sentences.n: The closing formula of an entry, as at 630: τῷ δ’ ἅμα ‘and with him’ (Thoas), τεσσαράκοντα ‘forty’, and μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο ‘black ships followed’, with μέλαιναι the feminine plural of μέλας ‘black’ and ἕποντο the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι.

sentences.t: Κρητῶν δ’ Ἰδομενεὺς δουρὶ κλυτὸς ἡγεμόνευεν,
sentences.l: And of the Cretans Idomeneus, famous with the spear, was leader,
sentences.i: And Idomeneus, famous with the spear, was leader of the Cretans,
sentences.n: The Cretans, in a new paragraph. Κρητῶν δ’ is ‘and of the Cretans’, with ἡγεμόνευεν ‘was leader’. δουρὶ κλυτός is ‘famous with the spear’: δουρί is the epic dative of δόρυ ‘spear’, giving the instrument, and κλυτός is ‘famous’, from κλύω ‘hear’, so ‘heard of’. The phrase is Idomeneus’ stock epithet, repeated at 650, and Tlepolemus has it at 657.

sentences.t:
οἳ Κνωσόν τ’ εἶχον Γόρτυνά τε τειχιόεσσαν,
Λύκτον Μίλητόν τε καὶ ἀργινόεντα Λύκαστον
Φαιστόν τε Ῥύτιόν τε, πόλεις εὖ ναιετοώσας,
sentences.l:
who held Cnossus and walled Gortyn,
Lyctus and Miletus and bright-white Lycastus,
and Phaestus and Rhytium, well-inhabited cities,
sentences.i: who held Cnossus and walled Gortyn, Lyctus, Miletus and bright-white Lycastus, Phaestus and Rhytium, well-inhabited cities,
sentences.n: The cities of Crete, all objects of εἶχον ‘held’. τειχιόεσσαν is ‘walled’, from τεῖχος ‘wall’, as of Tiryns at 559. ἀργινόεντα is ‘bright-white’; the word is built on ἀργός ‘bright, white’, the root also in ἀργής ‘bright’, and is said of places that gleam white, but its exact sense is not certain. Μίλητον is the Cretan Miletus, not the city in Ionia. πόλεις εὖ ναιετοώσας is ‘well-inhabited cities’, ναιετοώσας being the feminine accusative plural of ναιετάω ‘dwell’ with the stretched ending -όω-; the Greek has πόλεις here and ἄστεα ‘towns’ at 660.

sentences.t: ἄλλοι θ’ οἳ Κρήτην ἑκατόμπολιν ἀμφενέμοντο.
sentences.l: and the others, who inhabited around hundred-citied Crete.
sentences.i: and the others who inhabited the country around hundred-citied Crete.
sentences.n: ἄλλοι θ’ οἳ is ‘and the others who’, so that the cities named are only some of the island’s. ἑκατόμπολιν is ‘of a hundred cities’, from ἑκατόν ‘a hundred’ and πόλις, the stock epithet of Crete; ἀμφενέμοντο ‘inhabited around’ takes the island as its object, as at 574 and 585.

sentences.t:
τῶν μὲν ἄρ’ Ἰδομενεὺς δουρὶ κλυτὸς ἡγεμόνευε
Μηριόνης τ’ ἀτάλαντος Ἐνυαλίῳ ἀνδρειφόντῃ·
sentences.l:
Of these, then, Idomeneus, famous with the spear, was leader,
and Meriones, the equal of Enyalius, killer of men;
sentences.i: Of these, then, Idomeneus, famous with the spear, was the leader, and Meriones, the equal of Enyalius, killer of men;
sentences.n: Idomeneus’ second-in-command. The first half returns to 645, δουρὶ κλυτὸς ἡγεμόνευε, the verb now without its final ν; it is singular though two men are named, as at 563. Μηριόνης is ‘Meriones’, and ἀτάλαντος Ἐνυαλίῳ ἀνδρειφόντῃ is ‘the equal of Enyalius, killer of men’: ἀτάλαντος takes the dative, as at 627. Ἐνυάλιος is a war-god, usually identified with Ares, and ἀνδρειφόντης is built from ἀνήρ ‘man’ and the root of φόνος ‘killing’. Line 651 is metrically irregular as transmitted: its fifth foot is a spondee, and Ἐνυαλίῳ has to be scanned with synizesis, the -ιῳ as one syllable.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δ’ ἅμ’ ὀγδώκοντα μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο.
sentences.l: And with them eighty black ships followed.
sentences.i: And with them eighty black ships followed.
sentences.n: The closing formula of an entry, as at 568, here for the whole Cretan force: τοῖσι δ’ ἅμ’ ‘and with them’, plural because two commanders lead, ὀγδώκοντα ‘eighty’, μέλαιναι νῆες ἕποντο ‘black ships followed’.

sentences.t:
Τληπόλεμος δ’ Ἡρακλεΐδης ἠΰς τε μέγας τε
ἐκ Ῥόδου ἐννέα νῆας ἄγεν Ῥοδίων ἀγερώχων,
sentences.l:
And Tlepolemus, Heracles’-son, both good and great,
from Rhodes nine ships brought, of the lofty Rhodians,
sentences.i: And Tlepolemus, the son of Heracles, both good and great, brought nine ships from Rhodes, ships of the lofty Rhodians,
sentences.n: The Rhodians, in a new paragraph. Ἡρακλεΐδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Heracles’. ἠΰς is the epic form of ἐΰς ‘good’, in the sense of brave or noble, and μέγας ‘great’ says that he was big; together ἠΰς τε μέγας τε is ‘both good and great’. ἄγεν is the unaugmented imperfect of ἄγω ‘bring’, with νῆας ἐννέα ‘nine ships’, and ἐκ Ῥόδου is ‘from Rhodes’. Ῥοδίων ἀγερώχων is ‘of the lofty Rhodians’; ἀγέρωχος is a word whose meaning is not known, and the Odyssey, which uses it of Periclymenus, renders it ‘lofty’.

sentences.t:
οἳ Ῥόδον ἀμφενέμοντο διὰ τρίχα κοσμηθέντες
Λίνδον Ἰηλυσόν τε καὶ ἀργινόεντα Κάμειρον.
sentences.l:
who inhabited around Rhodes, arranged in three parts,
Lindus and Ialysus and bright-white Cameirus.
sentences.i: who inhabited the country around Rhodes, arranged in three parts: Lindus, Ialysus and bright-white Cameirus.
sentences.n: How the Rhodians lived. οἳ … ἀμφενέμοντο is ‘who inhabited around’, with Ῥόδον as object. διὰ τρίχα κοσμηθέντες is ‘arranged in three parts’: τρίχα is an adverb, ‘in three’ (compare τριχθά at 668), and κοσμηθέντες is the aorist passive participle of κοσμέω ‘set in order’. The three parts are named by the three cities, accusatives in apposition: Λίνδον, Ἰηλυσόν and ἀργινόεντα Κάμειρον, which has the same epithet as Lycastus at 647.

sentences.t:
τῶν μὲν Τληπόλεμος δουρὶ κλυτὸς ἡγεμόνευεν,
ὃν τέκεν Ἀστυόχεια βίῃ Ἡρακληείῃ,
sentences.l:
Of these Tlepolemus, famous with the spear, was leader,
whom bore Astyocheia to the might of Heracles,
sentences.i: Of these Tlepolemus, famous with the spear, was leader, whom Astyocheia bore to the might of Heracles,
sentences.n: τῶν μέν is ‘of these’, and δουρὶ κλυτὸς ἡγεμόνευεν is the epithet and verb of 645. ὃν τέκεν Ἀστυόχεια is ‘whom Astyocheia bore’, τέκεν the unaugmented aorist of τίκτω. βίῃ Ἡρακληείῃ is the dative of βίη ‘might’ with the adjective Ἡρακληείη ‘of Heracles’, a periphrasis for Heracles himself, ‘the might of Heracles’, and the dative says she bore him to Heracles.

sentences.t:
τὴν ἄγετ’ ἐξ Ἐφύρης ποταμοῦ ἄπο Σελλήεντος
πέρσας ἄστεα πολλὰ διοτρεφέων αἰζηῶν.
sentences.l:
whom he brought for himself from Ephyre, from the river Selleis,
having sacked many towns of Zeus-nurtured vigorous men.
sentences.i: whom he had brought from Ephyre, from the river Selleis, after sacking many towns of Zeus-nurtured, vigorous men.
sentences.n: Who Astyocheia was. τὴν is the relative ‘whom’, the article used as a pronoun. ἄγετ’ is ἄγετο, the unaugmented imperfect middle of ἄγω, ‘brought for himself’, the middle being the one used of taking a woman home; the subject, Heracles, is understood from the end of 658. ποταμοῦ ἄπο Σελλήεντος is ‘from the river Selleis’, with ἄπο placed after its noun. πέρσας is the aorist participle of πέρθω ‘sack’, and ἄστεα ‘towns’ the epic plural. διοτρεφέων is ‘Zeus-nurtured’ (epic genitive plural -έων), as the Odyssey translates it, and αἰζηῶν ‘vigorous men’, vigorous young men in their prime.

sentences.t:
Τληπόλεμος δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν τράφ’ ἐνὶ μεγάρῳ εὐπήκτῳ,
αὐτίκα πατρὸς ἑοῖο φίλον μήτρωα κατέκτα
ἤδη γηράσκοντα Λικύμνιον ὄζον Ἄρηος·
sentences.i: And when Tlepolemus had been reared in the well-framed hall, he killed at once the dear mother’s brother of his own father, Licymnius, scion of Ares, who was already growing old;
sentences.n: The killing that drove him out. ἐπεὶ οὖν is ‘when, then’, and τράφ’ is the elided τράφε, an unaugmented aorist of τρέφω in its intransitive sense, ‘was reared’ (θρέψε at 548 is the same verb). ἐνὶ μεγάρῳ εὐπήκτῳ is ‘in the well-framed hall’, εὔπηκτος being built on εὖ and πήγνυμι ‘fix, fit together’. αὐτίκα is ‘at once’ and κατέκτα the epic aorist of κατακτείνω ‘kill’. πατρὸς ἑοῖο is ‘of his own father’, ἑοῖο being the possessive, and μήτρως is ‘mother’s brother’, so Licymnius is the brother of Heracles’ mother. ἤδη γηράσκοντα is ‘already growing old’. ὄζον Ἄρηος is ‘scion of Ares’, as of Elephenor at 540.

sentences.t:
αἶψα δὲ νῆας ἔπηξε, πολὺν δ’ ὅ γε λαὸν ἀγείρας
βῆ φεύγων ἐπὶ πόντον·
sentences.l:
and quickly he built ships, and a great people having gathered
he went, fleeing, over the open-sea;
sentences.i: and quickly he built ships, and gathering a great many people he went in flight over the sea;
sentences.n: αἶψα is ‘quickly’, kept apart from αὐτίκα ‘at once’ in 662. νῆας ἔπηξε is ‘built ships’, ἔπηξε the aorist of πήγνυμι ‘fix, put together’. πολὺν … λαὸν ἀγείρας is ‘having gathered a great people’, ὅ γε being ‘he’ with stress and ἀγείρας the aorist participle of ἀγείρω ‘gather’; here λαός is a band of followers, not yet an army. βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω ‘go’, φεύγων ‘fleeing’, and ἐπὶ πόντον ‘over the open sea’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of 665.

sentences.t:
ἀπείλησαν γάρ οἱ ἄλλοι
υἱέες υἱωνοί τε βίης Ἡρακληείης.
sentences.l:
for they threatened him, the others,
sons and grandsons of the might of Heracles.
sentences.i: for the others, the sons and grandsons of the might of Heracles, had threatened him.
sentences.n: Why he fled. ἀπείλησαν is the aorist of ἀπειλέω ‘threaten’, and οἱ the enclitic dative ‘him’; γάρ links the threat to the flight just told, though the Greek does not name the killing as the cause. ἄλλοι ‘the others’ qualifies υἱέες υἱωνοί τε ‘sons and grandsons’, the remaining family of Heracles, and βίης Ἡρακληείης is the periphrasis of 658 in the genitive, ‘of the might of Heracles’. The unit begins in the middle of line 665.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἐς Ῥόδον ἷξεν ἀλώμενος ἄλγεα πάσχων·
sentences.l: But he to Rhodes came, wandering, suffering pains;
sentences.i: But he came to Rhodes, wandering and suffering pains;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ is ‘but he’, ἐς Ῥόδον ‘to Rhodes’, and ἷξεν the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘come’. ἀλώμενος ‘wandering’ is the participle of ἀλάομαι, and ἄλγεα πάσχων ‘suffering pains’ is the phrase the Odyssey uses of its hero.

sentences.t:
τριχθὰ δὲ ᾤκηθεν καταφυλαδόν, ἠδὲ φίληθεν
ἐκ Διός, ὅς τε θεοῖσι καὶ ἀνθρώποισιν ἀνάσσει,
καί σφιν θεσπέσιον πλοῦτον κατέχευε Κρονίων.
sentences.l:
And in three parts they settled, tribe by tribe, and were loved
by Zeus, who over gods and men is lord,
and on them wondrous riches poured down the son of Cronus.
sentences.i: And they settled in three parts, tribe by tribe, and were loved by Zeus, who is lord over gods and men, and the son of Cronus poured wondrous riches down on them.
sentences.n: What became of the Rhodians. τριχθά is ‘in three parts’ (an adverb, like τρίχα at 655), and καταφυλαδόν is ‘tribe by tribe’, from κατὰ φυλάς. ᾤκηθεν and φίληθεν are aorist passives of οἰκέω ‘settle’ and φιλέω ‘love’, with the epic ending -θεν for -θησαν; ἐκ Διός is ‘by Zeus’. ὅς τε is ‘who’, the epic τε marking a familiar fact, and ἀνάσσει ‘is lord’ takes the datives θεοῖσι καὶ ἀνθρώποισιν ‘over gods and men’. σφιν is the enclitic dative ‘to them’; θεσπέσιον πλοῦτον is ‘wondrous riches’, the object of κατέχευε, the epic augmented aorist of καταχέω ‘pour down’ (Attic κατέχεε). Κρονίων is ‘the son of Cronus’, Zeus again.

sentences.t:
Νιρεὺς αὖ Σύμηθεν ἄγε τρεῖς νῆας ἐΐσας
Νιρεὺς Ἀγλαΐης υἱὸς Χαρόποιό τ’ ἄνακτος
Νιρεύς, ὃς κάλλιστος ἀνὴρ ὑπὸ Ἴλιον ἦλθε
τῶν ἄλλων Δαναῶν μετ’ ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα·
sentences.l:
And Nireus, in turn, from Syme brought three well-balanced ships,
Nireus, son of Aglaie and of Charopus, the lord,
Nireus, who, the fairest man, beneath Ilium came
of the other Danaans, after the blameless son of Peleus;
sentences.i: And Nireus, in turn, brought three well-balanced ships from Syme, Nireus, the son of Aglaie and of lord Charopus, Nireus, who was the most beautiful man to come to Ilium of the other Danaans, after the blameless son of Peleus;
sentences.n: Nireus, in a new paragraph, with his name at the head of three lines running; both English layers keep all three. Νιρεὺς αὖ is ‘Nireus, in turn’, Σύμηθεν ‘from Syme’ (suffix -θεν), and ἄγε the unaugmented imperfect of ἄγω ‘bring’. ἐΐσας ‘well-balanced’ is the same epithet as νῆας ἐΐσας at 1.306, and its sense is not certain. Ἀγλαΐης is the genitive of Ἀγλαΐη, Χαρόποιο the epic genitive of Χάροπος, and ἄνακτος ‘lord’ agrees with Χαρόποιο; τε links the two parents. κάλλιστος is ‘fairest, most beautiful’, as in the Odyssey, and ὑπὸ Ἴλιον ἦλθε ‘came to Ilium’. The last line is also Odyssey 11.470, said of Ajax: ‘the blameless son of Peleus’ is Achilles.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἀλαπαδνὸς ἔην, παῦρος δέ οἱ εἵπετο λαός.
sentences.l: but he was feeble, and a scanty people followed him.
sentences.i: but he was feeble, and the troops that followed him were few.
sentences.n: The sting at the end of the entry. ἀλαπαδνός is ‘feeble, weak’. ἔην is the epic ἦν, and παῦρος ‘few, scanty’ agrees with the singular collective λαός, ‘people’, here a small following. οἱ is the enclitic dative ‘him’, and εἵπετο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ with the augment, unlike the unaugmented ἕποντο of the closing formula elsewhere; the entry has no such formula and gives no number of ships beyond the three of 671.
